The so-called Judges' Bill of 1925 fundamentally redefined the Supreme Court's role within the federal judiciary by repealing much of the mandatory jurisdiction of the Court. The act preserved an automatic right of appeal to the Supreme Court in a few types of cases, but in other areas cases would come to the Court only when the justices granted a writ of certiorari in response to a petition from a party in a case before a lower court. With authority to determine a greater number of the cases it heard, the Supreme Court became primarily a forum for deciding questions of constitutional principle, while the circuit courts of appeals issued the final decisions in the great majority of appeals cases.

At the same time that Chief Justice Taft led the effort to establish a judicial conference that would contribute to the more efficient administration of the lower federal courts, he and a committee of justices drafted legislation intended to ease the growing caseload of the Supreme Court. Earlier restrictions on appeals to the Supreme Court proved ineffective in the face of increased federal litigation associated with the First World War and the enforcement of Prohibition. The chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee formally requested the justices to draft legislation that might remedy the backlog of cases, although the suggestion for the bill came privately from Taft. Justice Willis Van Devanter headed the committee that referred the draft to the full Court before submitting it to Congress in late 1921.

The bill offered by the justices (thus its familiar title, the "Judges' Bill") eliminated direct appeals from the district courts to the Supreme Court except in certain cases related to interstate commerce and anti-trust legislation, writs of errors by the United States in criminal cases, reviews of rulings of the Interstate Commerce Commission, and injunctions against state administrative agencies. Appeals from the states' highest courts to the Supreme Court were limited to cases in which the state court declared an act of the United States invalid or denied a claim that a state law was unconstitutional. Other appeals from the state courts would be by petition for certiorari. Rulings of the U.S. courts of appeals could be appealed to the Supreme Court in cases where a state statute was declared invalid. No other decisions of the courts of appeals could be taken to the Supreme Court except by certiorari, although an appellate court could certify a case for a ruling from the Supreme Court. The bill also sought to bring together in a more logical and unified form legislation related to appeals from territorial courts and the Court of Claims.

After taking an unusually public role in his advocacy of the Conference of Senior Circuit Judges, Taft deferred to the advice of friends in Congress and allowed Van Devanter to represent the Court in committee hearings in the Senate and House of Representatives. Taft meanwhile cultivated support among the state bar associations and legal scholars. Although Congress did not act immediately on the recommended bill, by late 1924 a solid majority had coalesced behind the measure, which won approval in February 1925.

🪬Up or down? The New Dividing Line in Politics and Civilization🪬

Markku Siira

The traditional political division into the right and left has lost its power of explanation. In its place is a new, more vertically oriented question: Do we strive up to heaven or do we hold on to the earth? It is no longer just about economic policy, but about the orientation of the entire human civilization.

What if the political compass only pointed upwards and down? A prediction formulated in the 1970s has returned to the academic and technology debate in recent years. Iranian-American futurist Fereidoun M. Esfandiary, later known as FM-2030, in his writing Up-Wingers: A Futurist Manifesto (1973) argued that the division into right and left would be replaced by a split into an upper wing and a lower wings.

The vision of FM-2030 was meant literally. The upper wing looked to the sky, striving for a maximization of technological progress and wanting to overcome the natural boundaries of man. The lower wing turned its gaze to the earth, saw a danger in the crossing of borders and regarded these boundaries as characteristics of humanity. The colour world also changed: red and blue were replaced by black and green. Black refers to the so-called black sky thinking, the “Black sky thinking”, according to which the entire universe is to be transformed into a habitat for humans. Green, in turn, embodies an ecological consciousness whose roots lie in deep ecology and respect for the limits of nature. Today, this prediction no longer seems like a futuristic oddity, but almost like a prophecy.

In the United States, this dividing line has become the most acute. When Marc Andreessen, co-founder of the web browser Netscape and one of Silicon Valley's most influential investors, published a techno-optimistic manifesto in October 2023, he not only defended the technology, but declared it sacred. “Technology is the glory of human ambitions and human achievements, the spearhead of progress, and the realization of our potential,” he wrote. All claims that technology destroy jobs exacerbate inequality or endanger humanity, he described as lies.

Andreessen's manifesto embodies an extreme thinking of the upper wing: effective accelerationism (effective accelerationism) that calls for unrestricted technological progress. In his view, a slowdown in artificial intelligence is murder because it prevents preventable deaths. The New York Times columnist Elizabeth Spiers described the manifesto as confused and contradictory, comparing its mood to that of the manifesto of eco-terrorist Theodore Kaczynski, the “unabomber” – albeit without its ideological consequence.

The upper wing, however, is not exclusively libertarian. According to Steve Fuller, the “black up-wingers” unite the old libertarian right with the old technocratic left. They do not shy away from a role of the state if it serves technological progress. James Pethokoukis, a researcher at the American Enterprise Institute and host of the podcast Faster, Please!, is among the most prominent popularizers of this thinking. He regards the separation into an upper and a lower wing as America's most important political issue. In his view, the upper wing accelerates technological development, solves major problems and creates opportunities for all Americans. The lower wing, on the other hand, counters changes with caution, emphasizes the acceptance of borders and sees technological development primarily as a threat.

According to Pethokoukis, the “great slowdown” that began in the 1970s – the age of oil crisis, environmental regulation, and thinking within the limits of growth – led the U.S. economy to almost half that of it today, when it continued the growth rate of 1955 to 1973. The darker side of the upper wing is evident in its relationship to democracy. Pethokoukis describes the American economy as a living supercomputer weighing 21 trillion dollars and as a technological-organic organism, whose primary purpose is to process information through the reorganization of matter. In this vision, citizens appear as educated and healthy individuals who produce complex and information-rich creative thinking through networks. On the other hand, people are reduced to components of a computer that are useful for as long as you need it.

In Europe, attitudes towards technology are more cautious. When Andreessen published his manifesto, the leading European venture capital company XAnge did not counter the European technology, but demanded responsibility. Technology is not omnipotent and must interact with society instead of rising above it. This is not thinking of the lower wing in the depth ecological sense, but it is critical of the extremely technological solution approach of the upper wing.

The European Union has taken a more cautious course. The AI regulation of the EU and its quest for technological sovereignty embody a thinking that technological development is not an end in itself, but must be democratically controlled. The German cultural magazine Blätter noted that the technology in Andreessen's manifesto replaces democratic decision-making with its imperative application. In Germany, the dividing line is also evident in the party landscape. The rise of the AfD and the success of the left in Berlin in the 2026 elections show that the traditional center is losing support to both margins.

In China, the tension does not run in the same way between two wings, as the state plays a central role in managing technological development. When Dario Amodei, chairman of the board of Anthropic, proposed slowing the development of artificial intelligence and restricting China’s progress in the field, State Department spokesman Guo Jiakun said artificial intelligence was an extraordinarily important technology for the well-being of all humanity, and all sides should promote open and inclusive development.

The Chinese newspaper Global Times described Amodei's proposal as inappropriate, unfounded and hostile. China's approach resembles a state-directed upper wing in which security and social stability take precedence. China has long had strict AI regulations, such as a ban on deepfakes and restrictions to protect children. Beijing does not reject technology, but subordinates its development to political and societal goals.

The most radical form of the upper wing is found in long-termism, a thinking geared towards the long-term future, which has spread particularly in the environment of effective altruism. The hypothesis of the vulnerable world of AI philosopher Nick Bostrom states that technological development could reach a point where civilization would be destroyed without extreme global surveillance. According to Bostrom, the overall ability to ward off such dangers would require comprehensive real-time monitoring. He designs a system of “freedom tags” in which all citizens would wear a device equipped with cameras and microphones around their necks, which continuously transmits video and audio data to the cloud for analysis by artificial intelligence. In the case of suspicious activities, the system would alert the “Freedom Authority” and cause it to intervene. This is the dystopian endpoint of the upper wing: to be saved, humanity must abandon its privacy and submit to unprecedented surveillance. In the name of future generations, the concrete suffering of the population living today is to be justified.

The lower wing is no longer represented by the traditional environmental movement alone. Its main economic policy is the post-growth movement, the so-called degrowth, which calls for an absolute reduction in material consumption and energy consumption. Degrowth is not a unified movement, but encompasses a spectrum from anarchist localism to eco-socialist visions. Some of their thinkers are skeptical of industrialism, while others advocate digital planning and automation to free people from unnecessary work. Common to the supporters of the movement is the conviction that the ideal of uninterrupted economic growth is incompatible with the limited sustainability of the earth.

Ecological economist Josh Farley has stated that the environmental and social costs of growth currently exceed its economic benefits and lead the obsession away from growth from the things that could contribute to human flourishing. The challenge of degrowth lies in its political fragmentation: its most radical forms also encounter resistance within the green movement and the left. According to an analysis by Prospect Magazine, the dispute between the green transition and the post-growth economy is a false juxtaposition: both camps include democratic and authoritarian, localist and globalist, as well as techno-optimistic and tech-sceptical currents.

In Finland, the youth organization of the party Die Finnen (Perussuomalaiset, PS) has formulated a thesis that combines the logic of the lower wing with a demographic forecast: The concern for climate change and a better world is meaningless when the Finns die out. In their view, the low birth rate of the Finns poses a greater existential threat than climate change or Russia. “If there are no future generations, the future has no meaning whatsoever,” she argues. The same logic with which deep-ecological movements establish radical action in favor of nature is reversed in order to defend national continuity.

Technology tensions are expressed differently in the different parts of the world. In the United States, the acceleration driven by private capital meets the demand of the security circles and some politicians for slowdown. In Europe, caution based on regulation and social responsibility wrestles with concerns about competitiveness and the pursuit of technological self-determination. In China, state-controlled development, whose borders are determined by security, stability and geopolitical competition, forms the central area of tension.

FM-2030 viewed an optimistic belief in technology as the only relevant perspective and was of the view that the bulk of intellectuals were paralyzed by puritanic guilt and self-doubt. The body of the thinker, who died in 2000, is waiting deep-frozen in the facilities of the Alcor Foundation in case the medicine of the future could one day bring him back to life. What kind of world might await him if this reawakenment ever succeeds? The upper wing promises infinity in the stars, but in his vision man has no intrinsic value: he is part of a technology-centered system in which his value is measured by his utility. The lower wing sees the destruction, but in its most radical interpretation humanity itself is the biggest problem.

Perhaps the darkest truth is that both wings are right in their own way. Technology can actually solve some problems. On the other hand, today’s civilization is destroying the foundations of life with increasing speed. A third possibility – a technological solution to the ecological crisis without human being losing its meaning – would require something that neither of the two wings seems to offer. The old left-right split asked who would receive what. The new dividing line asks what kind of future we are heading towards and for whom it is destined. This is a far more difficult question, to which neither the black upper nor the green lower wing offers an answer.

Ethiopia's Maritime Access: Existing Ports and Legal Arrangements

1. Port of Djibouti – Djibouti

Ethiopia's primary maritime gateway, handling approximately 90–95% of its maritime trade. 

Supported by bilateral agreements, modern highways, and the Addis Ababa–Djibouti railway. Despite high logistics costs, it provides established access to international markets.

2. Port of Berbera – Somaliland/Somalia

An alternative commercial gateway supported by DP World investments and improved road connections. Ethiopia's proposed 19% ownership stake in 2018 was never finalized.

 The controversial 2024 naval-access agreement raised sovereignty and diplomatic concerns.

3. Port of Lamu – Kenya

Part of the LAPSSET regional transport corridor. Initial port facilities and road connections are operational, while railway and pipeline infrastructure remain under development. Offers potential access for southern Ethiopia.

4. Port Sudan – Sudan

Historically provided an alternative outlet for northern Ethiopian trade. Currently constrained by Sudan's internal conflict, insecurity, and disrupted transport infrastructure.

5. Ports of Assab and Massawa – Eritrea

Historically served Ethiopian trade, including after Eritrea's independence in 1993. Operations ceased following the 1998–2000 border war. The 2018 rapprochement raised hopes of reopening, but no lasting operational agreement emerged.

 Future access requires bilateral negotiations respecting Eritrean sovereignty.

 Conclusion

Maritime Access Does Not Mean Territorial Ownership

Under UNCLOS Part X (Articles 124–132), Ethiopia has the right to seek access to and from the sea through agreed transit arrangements, but no right to annex territory, seize ports, or impose military bases on sovereign coastal states.

Ethiopia's principal challenges are logistics costs, infrastructure financing, dependence on Djibouti, and regional diplomatic tensions.

The issue is not the absence of maritime access, but how to diversify it through peaceful cooperation rather than territorial demands.

One Black girl per class, written into the charter of America's first nursing school like a supply order. Eighty years later a Boston school had it up to two, odd-numbered years only, and Barbara Nichols took one of those two seats.

She graduated in 1959, and in 1978 she was elected president of the American Nurses Association, which had deliberately barred Black nurses until 1964. Eighty years to move the number from one to two, and you tell me what we are supposed to call that.

The New England Hospital for Women and Children in Boston opened the first nurse training school in the United States, and its charter set the number of Black students it would take.

The number was one.

One Black student per class, and one Jewish student, and that was the arrangement written into the founding document of American nursing education. It was not a loophole or a local prejudice, it was the plan.

Eighty years later, across the same city, a different Boston nursing school was still counting.

Massachusetts Memorial Hospital School of Nursing took two Black girls, and only on odd-numbered years. On even years it took three Jewish girls instead, and everyone in the admissions office knew the rotation.

Eighty years of American progress moved the number from one to two, on alternate years.

The girl who came through the 1878 door was named Mary Eliza Mahoney. The girl who came through the odd-year door in the 1950s was named Barbara Nichols.

This is what happened in between them, and what it cost.

Start with Mahoney, because the week they named for her is why this story is being told at all.

She was eighteen when she started at the New England Hospital, in 1863, and the job was cook and cleaning woman and washerwoman. She scrubbed that building, hauled its laundry, cooked its meals, and emptied whatever needed emptying, and she did it for fifteen years while the nurses walked past her in the corridors.

Fifteen years. She was watching the whole time.

In 1878 they let her into the school. She was thirty-three years old, which was over the school's own stated age limit of thirty-one, and the likeliest reason they bent it is that she had already given them a decade and a half of her back.

The program ran sixteen months. Students worked from six in the morning until nine at night, and in what the school called their free time they did the laundry and the ironing and the cleaning.

She was already good at that part.

Forty-two students started with her. Four finished.

On the first of August, 1879, Mary Eliza Mahoney became the first Black woman in the United States to hold a professional nursing diploma. She had waited fifteen years for a sixteen-month course.

She spent the next thirty years as a private duty nurse, working East Coast households, building the kind of reputation that travels by word of mouth among families who can afford to be particular. In 1908 she helped found the National Association of Colored Graduate Nurses, because the profession's main organization had made it clear what Black nurses could expect there.

In 1920, at seventy-five, she was among the first women in Boston to register to vote.

Three years later she was diagnosed with breast cancer, and she went for treatment to the New England Hospital for Women and Children. She died there in 1926, in the building where she had scrubbed the floors, at eighty years old.

Now the part that made her founding of the NACGN necessary.

In 1916, the American Nurses Association changed its membership rule. A nurse could no longer join through her nursing school's alumnae association, and instead had to go through her state association, which became the gatekeeper.

Sixteen states of the old Confederacy, plus the District of Columbia, refused Black members outright.

So a Black nurse in Alabama could hold a license, run a ward, and have no route whatsoever into the national body that spoke for her profession. She could not vote in it, could not be heard in it, could not appear in its count.

The association has since put the sentence in writing itself. Its Racial Reckoning Statement, adopted unanimously by its governing body in June of 2022, says that from 1916 until 1964 the ANA had "purposefully, systemically and systematically excluded Black nurses."

Forty-eight years. The last holdout, a district in Louisiana, did not drop its rule until 1964.

And in the North, where there was no law about it, the schools handled it with arithmetic. The historian Darlene Clark Hine, whose work the ANA cites in that same statement, found that "most of the hospital nursing schools in the North imposed racial quotas" while the Southern schools simply refused.

Which brings us to a hotel in New Orleans, and the year 1939.

The woman at the center of it was Estelle Massey Riddle Osborne. She was the first Black nurse in the United States to earn a master's degree, she had run the nursing school at Homer G. Phillips in St. Louis, and she was then president of the NACGN.

By any measure the profession used, she was one of the most credentialed nurses in America.

The president of the ANA invited her to New Orleans to sit with the association's Advisory Council and discuss the status of Black nurses. The meeting was set for the St. Charles Hotel, a place with marble steps out front and six Corinthian columns and a white cupola you could see from across the city.

Black guests did not use the marble steps. Black guests used the service entrance around the side and rode the freight elevator up with the linens and the kitchen deliveries.

Osborne found out what the hotel required and went to the ANA president with it. She was not asking for a boycott or a speech, only for the head of American nursing to object to it, out loud, once.

What came back was an offer of company.

The ANA president said she would walk in through the service entrance too. She would ride the freight elevator with her, and then they would go upstairs and have the meeting about the status of Black nurses in America.

Sit with that for a second. The most educated Black nurse in the country, invited to speak for every Black nurse in the country, offered a companion on the way up through the delivery entrance instead of a single sentence of protest.

Osborne did not go.

She stayed away, and the Advisory Council met and discussed the status of Black nurses without one in the room, and the minutes of that meeting record whatever they record.

That was 1939.

In Waterville, Maine, that same year, a baby girl was born who would grow up to hold the office of the woman who made that offer.

Barbara Lauraine Nichols was raised in Portland, in a family that treated education and public service as debts rather than choices. Her mother liked to say the child had wanted to be a nurse before she could talk.

A public health nurse who was a friend of the family gave her a toy medical kit, and she worked on her dolls with it.

Then she got older and wanted something else entirely.

She wanted the stage. She was active in children's theater and she wanted to act for a living, and she said so plainly for the rest of her life, and she also said exactly why she let it go.

The parts written for Black actresses in the 1950s were maids, servants, and custodians. That was the whole menu.

She had watched the same arithmetic run off the screen too. A Black woman could hold a bachelor's degree in physics and get hired as a cook, because the degree was never what was being read.

Nursing had one thing those jobs did not. Nursing had a license.

A license is a piece of paper saying the state examined you and found you competent, and it keeps saying that whether or not anyone in the room wants it to. She wanted a credential that would argue for her in places she would never be allowed to stand.

So she took the odd-year seat.

She had exactly one Black classmate. She said it herself decades later, remembering a school that admitted "two blacks on odd-numbered years," which meant that in the entire building there was one other person who understood what her days were like.

She said the expectations placed on her there were low. She also said something colder and more interesting about it, which is that because there were only two of them, the usual stereotypes had no room to operate, and so she got judged on her actual work.

That is the trade a quota makes. It buys you a fair look in exchange for a guarantee that there will never be enough of you to change anything.

She started nursing in 1959, when penicillin was still being talked about as a miracle drug and hospital staff argued over whether CPR was something decent people should be doing.

Her first job was Boston Children's Hospital, specialty wards. She was the only Black registered nurse on the entire staff.

She named the reason she got hired without any softening, which was that she had gone to a white nursing school rather than one of the Black nursing schools, and the school name was the credential the hospital was actually reading. The quota that had limited her also, in the sick logic of the thing, certified her.

Then the Navy.

She served as head nurse at the U.S. Naval Hospital in St. Albans, Queens, a post almost no Black woman held in that era. The hospital around her ran on hard segregation.

The intensive care unit where she worked ran on less of it, because in an ICU the sorting tends to collapse under the emergency. Somebody is coding and nobody is checking the ward assignment first.

The Navy is also where she found the next wall, and this one was made of paper.

Every other nurse on her unit had a bachelor's degree. She had a hospital diploma, because a hospital diploma was what had been available to a Black girl in Boston in the 1950s, and now the thing she had been permitted to get was the thing holding her down.

Here is where the price starts, and this is the part the obituaries skip.

She went back and got the bachelor's, at Case Western Reserve in Cleveland, finishing in 1966. Then she followed her husband Larry to Madison, Wisconsin, where he had come for graduate school, and she took a job at St. Mary's Hospital.

Then she went back again and got a master's at the University of Wisconsin, while working.

Do the household math on those years. Identical twin sons, and a daughter named Nichelle born in Madison at the end of that decade, and Larry in graduate school and later working as a systems analyst for the school district.

A woman working hospital shifts, carrying coursework, with three children in the house, twice going back for degrees she had been locked out of the first time.

And somewhere inside those twenty years at the bedside she worked out the thing that decided everything after.

She had ideas and she would offer them and they would die in the room. She came to understand that the problem was not the idea and not the people listening, it was the chair.

A staff nurse with a suggestion gets nodded at. A head nurse, a supervisor, a director with the identical suggestion has to be answered, because the title makes the answer compulsory.

Nobody was ever going to invite her to apply for those jobs, and she was clear-eyed about why, and she stopped waiting for the invitation.

She applied herself. She usually got them.

In 1970, the Wisconsin Nurses Association, then a hundred years old, elected her president. She was the first Black nurse to lead any state nurses association anywhere in the country.

She had a newborn daughter and twin boys at home.

She did not treat it as an honorary post. She built a working relationship with the Wisconsin Medical Society and got a Joint Practice Committee out of it, which in plain terms means she put doctors and nurses at one table with equal standing.

Then she went national, and she should have known what was waiting.

Estelle Osborne had been the first Black nurse elected to the ANA board, in 1948. By the association's own accounting, twenty-two years passed before another Black nurse was elected to it.

In 1972, when Black nurses raised that gap at the ANA convention, they were told what the association considered itself to owe them. When the NACGN dissolved and folded in, the one surviving obligation was the continued awarding of the Mary Mahoney Award.

One medal, named for the woman who scrubbed floors for fifteen years to get sixteen months of school. That was the inheritance, and they said it out loud in a convention hall.

Barbara Nichols sat on that board for twelve years, by the association's count, before she ever stood for the presidency.

In 1978 they elected her.

She was the first Black person to hold the office in the association's history, and she was elected fourteen years after the last Louisiana district stopped keeping Black nurses out. Some of the delegates voting for her had been members during the exclusion, and some of them had been sitting in that 1972 hall.

She was re-elected in 1980 and served through 1982.

Now here is the part that shows what she was actually carrying. She did not quit her job.

Through the presidency she stayed on at St. Mary's Hospital in Madison as director of inservice education, running staff training, keeping a payroll position at a hospital in Wisconsin while she ran the national association.

And she traveled roughly twelve thousand miles a month, coast to coast, speaking for the profession.

Twelve thousand miles a month is four hundred miles a day, every day, for four years, on top of a full-time hospital job and three children. That is what the milestone cost, and nobody put it on the plaque.

She spent it on two things.

The first was the table, and she pushed ANA into formal collaboration with the American Medical Association and the American Hospital Association, so nurses sat in national policy rooms with physicians and hospital executives instead of being handed the decisions afterward. Her argument was blunt and she made it constantly, that "nurses are the ones at the bedside" watching what happens to people, and that watching should come with a vote.

The second was education, and this one does not resolve cleanly, and it belongs in the record anyway.

She committed the association to the baccalaureate degree as the standard for entering nursing. She called it "highly divisive, but essential," and she meant essential to nursing being treated as a profession rather than a trade.

Here is the shadow on it.

ANA had first taken that position in 1965. In the same 2022 statement where it confessed the exclusion, the association also acknowledged that raising the bar had the effect of disenfranchising the schools that were open to students of color, and shutting out the nurses those schools produced.

Barbara Nichols was a hospital diploma graduate. She was the product of exactly the kind of program that policy pushed to the margin, and she had to go back twice to collect the degrees the system would not credit her without.

She pushed the standard anyway, and the association now says the standard did harm. Both of those are true, and she spent decades afterward arguing for the credential and for the access to it in the same breath, which is the only honest place to stand.

On the twelfth of December, 1981, Estelle Massey Osborne died at eighty.

Barbara Nichols was sitting in the presidency at the time. The woman who had been offered a ride in the freight elevator lived to see a Black woman running the association that let it happen, and as far as the record shows, nobody thought to put the two of them in a photograph together.

Nichols kept working for another forty-four years.

In 1983 she was appointed secretary of the Wisconsin Department of Regulation and Licensing, the first Black woman in that state's history to hold a cabinet-level post, and she rewrote parts of Wisconsin's Nurse Practice Act from inside the building.

From 1999 to 2011 she ran the Commission on Graduates of Foreign Nursing Schools, checking credentials of nurses trained abroad, and she framed that job as two things at once. Protect patients from underprepared staff, and protect immigrant nurses from being worked as cheap labor once they landed.

She published more than two hundred papers and sat on the board of the International Council of Nurses.

And her daughter grew up.

Nichelle Nichols was born in Madison and graduated from Madison West High School in 1987. A few years later she was in California, single, with two children and a third coming, on public assistance.

She said it plainly in a 2015 interview, that she was "a single parent trying to go to college while working full time." Which is close to a description of her mother twenty-five years earlier, minus the safety net.

She turned it. Bachelor's, master's, then doctoral work, then seventeen years at Madison nonprofits, then engagement chief for the Madison School District, then president of the Madison School Board.

The ladder Barbara Nichols spent her life building did not automatically carry her own child up it. Her daughter had to climb the same way she did, one credential at a time, while working.

Nichols never stopped. At eighty-four she was testifying at the Wisconsin State Capitol on a bill about what advanced practice nurses may do without a physician standing over them, and at eighty-five she was in Montreal for an International Council of Nurses meeting, still working full time as executive director of the Wisconsin Center for Nursing.

She was asked around then what had actually changed since 1959. Her answer named the thing she had spent sixty-seven years pushing against, that "the battle of being the handmaiden of the physician persists."

Sixty-seven years, and she still had to say the word handmaiden.

Barbara L. Nichols died on the twenty-second of July, 2026, at eighty-seven years old.

Four days later, Black Nurses Week began. It runs from the twenty-sixth of July to the first of August, and the closing date is the day Mary Eliza Mahoney walked out of that Boston hospital in 1879 with her diploma.

She missed it by four days.

So keep the numbers, because the numbers are the entire story. One Black student per class written into the charter of the first nursing school in America, two on odd-numbered years eighty years later in the same city, forty-eight years of a locked door confessed in writing by the people who locked it, twenty-two years without a single Black nurse on the board, and one medal offered as the whole debt.

Two women were counted into Boston nursing schools eighty years apart, and one of them scrubbed the floors for fifteen years first, and the other one ended up running the profession.

The week starts on the twenty-sixth. When it comes around, put Mary Mahoney and Barbara Nichols in the same sentence, out loud, to somebody who does not know either name, because the record has managed a hundred and forty-seven years without once doing it.

The Art of War is an ancient Chinese military treatise dating from the late Spring and Autumn period (roughly 5th century BC). The work, which is attributed to the ancient Chinese military strategist Sun Tzu ("Master Sun"), is composed of 13 chapters. Each one is devoted to a different set of skills or art related to warfare and how it applies to military strategy and tactics. For almost 1,500 years, it was the lead text in an anthology that was formalized as the Seven Military Classics by Emperor Shenzong of Song in 1080. The Art of War remains the most influential strategy text in East Asian warfare,[1] has influenced both East Asian and Western military theory and thinking, and has found a variety of applications in myriad competitive non-military endeavors across the modern world including espionage,[2] culture, politics, business, and sports.[3][4][5][6]

The book contains a detailed explanation and analysis of the 5th-century BC Chinese military, from weapons, environmental conditions, and strategy to rank and discipline. Sun also stressed the importance of intelligence operatives and espionage to the war effort. Considered one of history's finest military tacticians and analysts, his teachings and strategies formed the basis of advanced military training throughout the world.

The book was translated into French and published in 1772 by the French priest Jesuit Jean Joseph Marie Amiot; it was re-published in 1782. A partial translation into English was attempted by British officer Everard Ferguson Calthrop in 1905 under the title The Book of War. The first annotated English translation was completed and published by Lionel Giles in 1910.[7] Military and political leaders such as the Chinese communist revolutionary Mao Zedong, Japanese daimyō Takeda Shingen, Vietnamese general Võ Nguyên Giáp, is cited along with American military generals Douglas MacArthur and Norman Schwarzkopf Jr. as having drawn inspiration from the book.[8]

Outside of military use, The Art of War has also become a source of inspiration in business, politics, sports and esports, and its usage has extended to film and television.

History
Text and commentaries
The Art of War is traditionally attributed to an ancient Chinese military general known as Sun Tzu (pinyin: Sūnzǐ), meaning 'Master Sun'. Sun Tzu is said to have lived in the 6th century BC, but the earliest parts of The Art of War probably date to at least 100 years later.[9]

Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, the first of China's 24 dynastic histories, records an early Chinese tradition that a text on military matters was written by one "Sun Wu" (孫武) from the State of Qi, and that this text had been read and studied by King Helü of Wu (r. 514–495 BC).[10] This text was traditionally identified with the received Master Sun's Art of War. The conventional view was that Sun Wu was a military theorist from the end of the Spring and Autumn period (776–471 BC) who fled his home state of Qi to the southeastern Kingdom of Wu, where he is said to have impressed the king with his ability to quickly train even court women in military discipline and to have made Wu's armies powerful enough to challenge their western rivals in the state of Chu. This view is still widely held in China.[11]

The strategist, poet, and warlord Cao Cao in the early 3rd century AD authored the earliest known commentary to the Art of War.[10] Cao's preface makes clear that he edited the text and removed certain passages, but the extent of his changes were unclear historically.[10] The Art of War appears throughout the bibliographical catalogs of the Chinese dynastic histories, but listings of its divisions and size varied widely.[10]

The Art of War is an ancient Chinese military treatise dating from the late Spring and Autumn period (roughly 5th century BC). The work, which is attributed to the ancient Chinese military strategist Sun Tzu ("Master Sun"), is composed of 13 chapters. Each one is devoted to a different set of skills or art related to warfare and how it applies to military strategy and tactics. For almost 1,500 years, it was the lead text in an anthology that was formalized as the Seven Military Classics by Emperor Shenzong of Song in 1080. The Art of War remains the most influential strategy text in East Asian warfare,[1] has influenced both East Asian and Western military theory and thinking, and has found a variety of applications in myriad competitive non-military endeavors across the modern world including espionage,[2] culture, politics, business, and sports.[3][4][5][6]

The book contains a detailed explanation and analysis of the 5th-century BC Chinese military, from weapons, environmental conditions, and strategy to rank and discipline. Sun also stressed the importance of intelligence operatives and espionage to the war effort. Considered one of history's finest military tacticians and analysts, his teachings and strategies formed the basis of advanced military training throughout the world.

The book was translated into French and published in 1772 by the French priest Jesuit Jean Joseph Marie Amiot; it was re-published in 1782. A partial translation into English was attempted by British officer Everard Ferguson Calthrop in 1905 under the title The Book of War. The first annotated English translation was completed and published by Lionel Giles in 1910.[7] Military and political leaders such as the Chinese communist revolutionary Mao Zedong, Japanese daimyō Takeda Shingen, Vietnamese general Võ Nguyên Giáp, is cited along with American military generals Douglas MacArthur and Norman Schwarzkopf Jr. as having drawn inspiration from the book.[8]

Outside of military use, The Art of War has also become a source of inspiration in business, politics, sports and esports, and its usage has extended to film and television.

History
Text and commentaries
The Art of War is traditionally attributed to an ancient Chinese military general known as Sun Tzu (pinyin: Sūnzǐ), meaning 'Master Sun'. Sun Tzu is said to have lived in the 6th century BC, but the earliest parts of The Art of War probably date to at least 100 years later.[9]

Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, the first of China's 24 dynastic histories, records an early Chinese tradition that a text on military matters was written by one "Sun Wu" (孫武) from the State of Qi, and that this text had been read and studied by King Helü of Wu (r. 514–495 BC).[10] This text was traditionally identified with the received Master Sun's Art of War. The conventional view was that Sun Wu was a military theorist from the end of the Spring and Autumn period (776–471 BC) who fled his home state of Qi to the southeastern Kingdom of Wu, where he is said to have impressed the king with his ability to quickly train even court women in military discipline and to have made Wu's armies powerful enough to challenge their western rivals in the state of Chu. This view is still widely held in China.[11]

The strategist, poet, and warlord Cao Cao in the early 3rd century AD authored the earliest known commentary to the Art of War.[10] Cao's preface makes clear that he edited the text and removed certain passages, but the extent of his changes were unclear historically.[10] The Art of War appears throughout the bibliographical catalogs of the Chinese dynastic histories, but listings of its divisions and size varied widely.[10]

The Art of War is an ancient Chinese military treatise dating from the late Spring and Autumn period (roughly 5th century BC). The work, which is attributed to the ancient Chinese military strategist Sun Tzu ("Master Sun"), is composed of 13 chapters. Each one is devoted to a different set of skills or art related to warfare and how it applies to military strategy and tactics. For almost 1,500 years, it was the lead text in an anthology that was formalized as the Seven Military Classics by Emperor Shenzong of Song in 1080. The Art of War remains the most influential strategy text in East Asian warfare,[1] has influenced both East Asian and Western military theory and thinking, and has found a variety of applications in myriad competitive non-military endeavors across the modern world including espionage,[2] culture, politics, business, and sports.[3][4][5][6]

The book contains a detailed explanation and analysis of the 5th-century BC Chinese military, from weapons, environmental conditions, and strategy to rank and discipline. Sun also stressed the importance of intelligence operatives and espionage to the war effort. Considered one of history's finest military tacticians and analysts, his teachings and strategies formed the basis of advanced military training throughout the world.

The book was translated into French and published in 1772 by the French priest Jesuit Jean Joseph Marie Amiot; it was re-published in 1782. A partial translation into English was attempted by British officer Everard Ferguson Calthrop in 1905 under the title The Book of War. The first annotated English translation was completed and published by Lionel Giles in 1910.[7] Military and political leaders such as the Chinese communist revolutionary Mao Zedong, Japanese daimyō Takeda Shingen, Vietnamese general Võ Nguyên Giáp, is cited along with American military generals Douglas MacArthur and Norman Schwarzkopf Jr. as having drawn inspiration from the book.[8]

Outside of military use, The Art of War has also become a source of inspiration in business, politics, sports and esports, and its usage has extended to film and television.

History
Text and commentaries
The Art of War is traditionally attributed to an ancient Chinese military general known as Sun Tzu (pinyin: Sūnzǐ), meaning 'Master Sun'. Sun Tzu is said to have lived in the 6th century BC, but the earliest parts of The Art of War probably date to at least 100 years later.[9]

Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian, the first of China's 24 dynastic histories, records an early Chinese tradition that a text on military matters was written by one "Sun Wu" (孫武) from the State of Qi, and that this text had been read and studied by King Helü of Wu (r. 514–495 BC).[10] This text was traditionally identified with the received Master Sun's Art of War. The conventional view was that Sun Wu was a military theorist from the end of the Spring and Autumn period (776–471 BC) who fled his home state of Qi to the southeastern Kingdom of Wu, where he is said to have impressed the king with his ability to quickly train even court women in military discipline and to have made Wu's armies powerful enough to challenge their western rivals in the state of Chu. This view is still widely held in China.[11]

The strategist, poet, and warlord Cao Cao in the early 3rd century AD authored the earliest known commentary to the Art of War.[10] Cao's preface makes clear that he edited the text and removed certain passages, but the extent of his changes were unclear historically.[10] The Art of War appears throughout the bibliographical catalogs of the Chinese dynastic histories, but listings of its divisions and size varied widely.[10]

In Revelation 21:1, John sees something spectacular: “Then I saw ‘a new heaven and a new earth,’ for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.” This new earth and new heaven are sometimes referred to as the “eternal state.” As seen in Revelation chapters 21—22, the new earth will be the eternal dwelling place of believers in Jesus Christ. Scripture gives us a few details of the new heaven and new earth.

The current heaven and earth have long been subject to God’s curse because of mankind’s sin. All creation “has been groaning as in the pains of childbirth” (Romans 8:22) as it awaits the fulfillment of God’s plan and “the children of God to be revealed” (verse 19). Heaven and earth will pass away (Mark 13:31), and they will be replaced by the new heaven and the new earth. At that time, the Lord, seated on His throne, says, “I am making everything new!” (Revelation 21:5). In the new creation, sin will be totally eradicated, and “there shall be no more curse” (Revelation 22:3, NKJV).

The new heaven and new earth are also mentioned in Isaiah 65:17; 66:22; and 2 Peter 3:13. Peter says that the new heaven and new earth will be “where righteousness dwells.” Isaiah says that “the former things will not be remembered, nor will they come to mind.” Things will be completely new, and the old order of things, with the accompanying sorrow and tragedy, will be gone.

The new earth will be free from sin, evil, sickness, suffering, and death. It will be earth as God originally intended it to be, prior to the curse of sin. It will be Eden restored.

A major feature of the new earth will be the New Jerusalem. John calls it “the Holy City . . . coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband” (Revelation 21:2). This glorious city, with its streets of gold and pearly gates, is situated on a new, glorious earth. The tree of life will be there (Revelation 22:2). This city represents the final state of redeemed mankind, forever in fellowship with God: “God’s dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. . . . His servants will serve him. They will see his face” (Revelation 21:3; 22:3–4).

In the new heaven and new earth, Scripture says, there are seven things notable for their absence—seven things that are “no more”:
• no more sea (Revelation 21:1)
• no more death (Revelation 21:4)
• no more mourning (Revelation 21:4)
• no more weeping (Revelation 21:4)
• no more pain (Revelation 21:4)
• no more curse (Revelation 22:3)
• no more night (Revelation 22:5)

The creation of the new heaven and new earth brings the promise that God “will wipe every tear from their eyes” (Revelation 21:4). This event comes after the tribulation, after the Lord’s second coming, after the millennial kingdom, after the final rebellion, after the final judgment of Satan, and after the great white throne judgment. The brief description of the new heaven and new earth is the last glimpse into eternity that the Bible gives.

text:
America First, Everyone Else Pays? Trump's Russian Oil Paradox and the Price of Geopolitical Loyalty

From pressuring India over Russian oil to easing restrictions on Russian diesel, Washington's latest decisions raise uncomfortable questions about sanctions, energy security, and the limits of American leadership.

There is a question the world should be asking Washington right now: If buying Russian energy is a threat to international security, why does that principle appear to change when American consumers need cheaper fuel?

For months, countries purchasing Russian oil have faced political pressure, economic penalties and warnings about the consequences of financing Moscow's war against Ukraine. India became one of the most prominent targets of that pressure. European countries have also struggled to balance their energy needs with their commitments to reduce dependence on Russia.

Yet, as fuel prices rise and the November 3, 2026, US midterm elections approach, President Donald Trump has endorsed an arrangement allowing Russian diesel supplies into international markets while easing certain sanctions. The move has attracted criticism from lawmakers in both American political parties and concern from Ukraine and European officials. The Kremlin, meanwhile, has suggested that the arrangement could open the door to broader economic cooperation between Washington and Moscow. Reuters, October 14, 2026

The contradiction is difficult to ignore. But to understand its implications, we must look beyond the immediate argument over fuel prices.

India's oil purchases: A question of principle or power?

India's decision to purchase Russian crude was driven by a straightforward economic calculation. As a major energy importer, India has a responsibility to secure supplies at competitive prices, protect its economy from external shocks and meet the needs of its population.

Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, discounted Russian crude became an important part of India's energy strategy. Indian refiners benefited from access to supplies that were commercially attractive, while Russian oil exports found alternative markets as Western restrictions reshaped global trade.

Washington objected to India's purchases and used trade pressure to influence New Delhi's decisions.

In August 2025, the Trump administration imposed an additional 25% tariff on Indian imports, explicitly linking it to India's Russian oil purchases. In February 2026, Trump removed that additional tariff after his administration stated that India had committed to stop directly or indirectly importing Russian oil and increase purchases of American energy products. White House, February 6–9, 2026

This sequence demonstrates that energy trade was not simply a matter of commercial exchange. It became a bargaining instrument in a wider relationship involving trade, national security and strategic alignment.

Washington was effectively telling New Delhi that its energy choices could carry economic consequences.

The United States was entitled to pursue its foreign-policy objectives. But India was equally entitled to evaluate the consequences of those objectives for its own economy.

The central issue is not whether India should purchase Russian oil indefinitely. It is whether a country's sovereign energy decisions should be treated as acceptable only when they align with the preferences of a more powerful partner.

That question becomes considerably more uncomfortable when Washington's own policies are examined.

The Russian diesel arrangement changes the conversation

The Trump administration's latest arrangement with Russia has brought the issue into sharper focus.

On October 12, Trump defended the deal amid criticism that easing restrictions on Russian diesel could conflict with American measures intended to restrict Russian energy revenues while Moscow continues its war against Ukraine. Trump argued that he was making the right choice for the American people and seeking to bring down fuel prices. Reuters also reported that the agreement had become politically sensitive ahead of the midterm elections. Reuters, October 12, 2026

There is an important distinction here. The arrangement should not automatically be described as an ordinary American purchase of Russian crude oil. The reporting concerns Russian diesel supplies intended for international markets, alongside the easing of certain sanctions. The precise commercial flows and beneficiaries matter.

Nevertheless, the strategic contradiction remains.

When India purchased Russian crude, Washington treated those purchases as a problem requiring economic pressure. Now, when Russian diesel supplies may help ease fuel-price pressures, the Trump administration is prepared to accommodate Russian energy exports.

The two transactions are not identical. India imports crude oil for refining, while diesel is a refined petroleum product, and the legal arrangements differ. But both raise a common question: how consistently is Washington applying its stated objective of restricting Russian energy revenues?

If Russian energy can be accommodated when doing so serves American economic interests, then the argument against other countries purchasing that energy cannot rest on principle alone. It must also be examined in terms of strategic priorities, economic costs and political convenience.

That is not proof that every American sanctions decision is hypocritical. It is a reason to demand a clearer explanation of the differences.

The Middle East: When geopolitical decisions reach the fuel pump

The timing makes this debate even more significant.

The Middle East remains central to the world's energy security. Oil and gas supplies, tanker movements, maritime chokepoints and critical infrastructure are all vulnerable to regional conflict. When shipping routes become dangerous or pipelines are damaged, the consequences extend far beyond the immediate battlefield.

The expanding conflict involving Iran, attacks on maritime traffic and disruptions to regional infrastructure have demonstrated how quickly security crises can become economic crises.

In September 2026, Saudi Arabia temporarily shut its East-West oil pipeline following a drone attack. The pipeline had become especially important because it allowed Saudi crude to reach the Red Sea without passing through the Strait of Hormuz. The disruption threatened a route carrying an estimated four to five million barrels of oil per day in the preceding months. Reuters reporting, September 12, 2026

Houthi advances and threats to Red Sea shipping added another layer of uncertainty. But it is important not to conflate these developments: the pipeline attack was attributed by Saudi and Iraqi authorities to a drone originating in Iraq, while Houthi activity presented additional threats to maritime traffic.

Saudi Arabia subsequently restored pipeline operations towards approximately 5.8 million barrels per day by October 6, according to reporting published on October 12. The disruption nevertheless exposed the vulnerability of the infrastructure on which global energy markets depend. The National, October 12, 2026

The lesson is straightforward: energy security cannot be separated from military strategy.

When a conflict threatens oil production, pipelines or shipping, the consequences include higher transport costs, increased insurance premiums, supply uncertainty and pressure on fuel prices. Those costs eventually reach businesses and households.

This is precisely why governments cannot treat energy decisions as though they exist in isolation from their wider foreign policies.

If Washington pursues a military strategy that contributes to regional instability, it must also confront the economic consequences of that strategy. It cannot simply demand that other countries absorb the costs while presenting its own efforts to secure cheaper supplies as an entirely separate matter.

The precise contribution of any particular military action to fuel prices must be established with evidence. But the broader relationship between conflict, supply disruptions and energy costs is undeniable.

Ukraine: Can Kyiv depend on Washington's changing priorities?

The implications extend beyond oil.

Ukraine's war effort has depended significantly on Western military assistance, intelligence sharing, financial support and diplomatic backing. The United States has been a particularly important actor in that relationship.

But the relationship between Washington and Kyiv has become increasingly complicated as Trump has pursued negotiations with Moscow and demanded changes in Ukraine's approach to the conflict.

On October 11, Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. Subsequent reports of strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure raised questions about whether the announcement had produced a mutually accepted and enforceable arrangement. The distinction matters: an announcement by a mediator is not equivalent to a formal agreement accepted and implemented by both sides.

On October 13, Trump maintained that the United States was still sharing intelligence with Ukraine and working to end the war. He also defended the Russian diesel arrangement. Reuters, October 13, 2026

For Kyiv, the problem is strategic uncertainty.

A country at war must plan around the reliability of its military supplies, intelligence partnerships and diplomatic commitments. If the policies of its most important partner change according to that partner's domestic economic priorities, Ukraine has reason to reconsider the degree to which it can depend on Washington.

This does not mean Ukraine should abandon negotiations with the United States. Nor does it establish that American support has become worthless. It means Ukraine must distinguish between support based on enduring strategic commitments and support that may be conditional on changing political calculations.

That is a difficult distinction, but an essential one.

Trump has also called for Ukrainian elections. Whether and when elections can be held must be assessed under Ukrainian law, wartime conditions and the practical requirements of a free and fair vote.

Ukrainians, not the American president, must determine their country's political leadership through a legitimate process.

Washington can express preferences, offer assistance and exert diplomatic pressure. But publicly demanding a change of leadership creates a legitimate concern about the boundary between diplomatic influence and interference in another country's domestic politics.

It would be premature to conclude that Trump intends to install a puppet president. Such an allegation requires evidence of an actual plan or intervention. Nevertheless, the principle is clear: an election cannot be considered genuinely democratic if its outcome is expected to satisfy an external power rather than the electorate.

Ukraine's political future belongs to Ukrainians.

Is Trump trying to protect his domestic political position?

The November 3 midterm elections provide another important part of the context.

Fuel prices are politically sensitive in the United States. Diesel affects freight transport, agricultural operations, logistics and the cost of goods. When fuel becomes more expensive, businesses face higher operating costs, and those costs can feed into prices paid by consumers.

A president who promises economic relief therefore has a strong incentive to pursue policies that can reduce energy costs.

Trump's defence of the Russian diesel arrangement, combined with reporting that explicitly links rising fuel prices to Republican electoral concerns, makes domestic political pressure a reasonable part of the analysis.

But there is a difference between identifying a political incentive and proving a political motive.

We cannot establish from timing alone that the arrangement was primarily designed to win the midterms. Lowering fuel prices may be a genuine economic objective, even if the political benefits are obvious.

What we can say is that the arrangement creates a potential political advantage for Trump while raising difficult questions about the consistency of his Russia policy.

There is also a constitutional point worth remembering. Losing control of Congress would weaken a president's ability to advance legislation and could increase oversight and investigations. It would not automatically remove him from office. Impeachment by the House and removal following a Senate conviction are separate constitutional processes, with removal requiring a two-thirds vote of senators present.

The electoral calculation is therefore relevant, but it should not be exaggerated into a claim that Trump's presidency necessarily depends on retaining both chambers.

The more important question is whether short-term domestic political pressures are beginning to shape decisions with long-term consequences for America's international credibility.

Europe faces its own energy dilemma

Europe's position deserves equal attention.

Following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, European governments worked to reduce their dependence on Russian fossil fuels. They expanded alternative supply arrangements, increased imports from other producers and invested in infrastructure and energy diversification.

Those decisions carried costs. Alternative supplies can involve longer transport routes, different contract structures, additional infrastructure requirements and exposure to global market competition.

But the policy was not based solely on the immediate price of a barrel of oil or a unit of gas. It also reflected concerns about strategic dependence and the risk that Russia could use energy supplies as a political instrument.

That context must not be ignored.

Nevertheless, Europe has every right to examine whether its energy policies remain economically sustainable and strategically effective. If Washington can accommodate Russian diesel supplies when American consumers face high prices, European governments are entitled to ask whether their own policies are delivering the right balance between affordability, security and political objectives.

Why should Europe bear a disproportionate economic burden if other powers are prepared to make exceptions when their interests demand it?

The answer cannot simply be that Europe must follow Washington.

Nor should it automatically be that Europe must resume buying Russian energy. Russian gas and oil are different markets, European infrastructure and contracts vary, and existing restrictions can make particular transactions illegal or impractical. A return to Russian supplies could also recreate strategic vulnerabilities that European governments have spent years trying to reduce.

The proper question is not whether Europe should obey the United States or ignore it. It is whether European governments are making independent, evidence-based decisions that serve European citizens.

That means comparing actual delivered costs, legal restrictions, supply reliability, infrastructure capacity and the strategic risks associated with each supplier.

Strategic autonomy means having the capacity to make your own decisions, not simply reversing another country's decisions.

What about the possibility of a larger bargain behind closed doors?

It is reasonable to ask whether the Russian diesel arrangement forms part of a wider understanding between Washington and Moscow.

Energy transactions can be connected to negotiations over sanctions, the war in Ukraine, investment, minerals, trade and security. The Kremlin's public suggestion that the diesel arrangement could lead to broader economic cooperation makes that possibility worth investigating.

But suspicion is not proof.

We should not assume that a secret bargain exists merely because the public explanations appear inconsistent. To establish a wider agreement, we would need evidence such as official documents, corroborated reporting, confirmed negotiations or clearly connected policy decisions.

Until then, the defensible conclusion is narrower: the arrangement demonstrates that Washington is willing to reconsider certain restrictions on Russian energy when it believes doing so serves its interests.

That alone is significant.

It raises questions about whether sanctions are being treated as instruments of a consistent long-term strategy or as bargaining tools that can be adjusted when economic and political circumstances change.

If sanctions can be relaxed for one transaction while other countries continue to face pressure over related energy purchases, Washington owes its partners a clear explanation of the distinction.

India must draw its own strategic lessons

For India, the implications extend beyond the immediate question of Russian oil.

India maintains relationships with the United States, Russia, Europe and countries across the Middle East. Its energy security depends on diversified supplies, affordable imports, stable shipping routes and the ability to protect its economic interests amid international competition.

New Delhi should therefore resist the temptation to frame this debate solely as a contest between Washington and Moscow.

The objective should be to preserve India's freedom of decision-making while avoiding unnecessary economic exposure to any single supplier or strategic partner.

That requires diversification, investment in domestic energy capabilities, resilient maritime trade routes and a foreign policy grounded in India's own interests.

It also requires realism about the costs of strategic choices. Dependence on discounted oil can create economic advantages, but sanctions, trade restrictions and geopolitical shocks can offset those benefits.

The lesson is not that India should always purchase Russian oil or that it should reject American pressure in every circumstance.

It is that India must retain the ability to evaluate each decision on its own merits rather than allowing another country's shifting priorities to determine its energy policy.

The real test of American leadership

The United States remains a major economic, military and diplomatic power. Its relationships with India, Europe and Ukraine matter for reasons that extend far beyond a single oil transaction.

But leadership requires more than the ability to impose costs on other countries. It requires a degree of consistency between a government's stated principles and its own decisions.

If Washington argues that Russian energy purchases undermine international security, it must explain why certain Russian energy transactions can be accommodated when American fuel prices become politically difficult.

If Washington expects Europe to accept economic costs in pursuit of strategic objectives, it must recognise Europe's right to assess those costs independently.

If Washington wants Ukraine to make difficult concessions in pursuit of peace, it must acknowledge that Ukraine's sovereignty and political legitimacy cannot simply be subordinated to American preferences.

And if Washington expects India to make energy decisions that carry economic consequences for its own population, it must recognise that India has national interests of its own.

None of this means that every country faces identical circumstances or that every policy should be the same. Different products, legal frameworks, security risks and economic conditions can justify different decisions.

But those differences must be explained rather than concealed behind slogans.

Trump's approach to Russian diesel, India's energy trade, the war in Ukraine and Europe's energy dilemma exposes a larger challenge for the international system: the tension between universal principles and the national interests of powerful states.

The answer is not to assume that Washington can never be trusted, nor to conclude that every American decision is motivated by domestic politics.

It is to recognise that no major power's interests should be mistaken for the interests of the entire international community.

For India and Europe, the task is to pursue energy security without surrendering strategic autonomy. For Ukraine, it is to seek peace without sacrificing sovereignty. For Washington, it is to demonstrate that its policies are guided by more than the immediate political advantages of the moment.

Ultimately, the credibility of American leadership will not be determined by how forcefully it demands that others follow its policies.

It will be determined by whether those policies remain defensible when the United States itself faces the same economic pressures it asks others to endure.

When Russian energy is unacceptable for another country but negotiable when American fuel prices rise, the world is entitled to ask a simple question: is this a consistent strategy or is it America First, regardless of who pays the price?

POLITICAL CONSISTENCY ABOVE ALL

Tonatiuh Cuazitl

Vanessa Rubio proposes distinguishing between what Mexico cannot control, what it can influence in its relationship with the United States, and what depends on its own domestic agenda. I agree with that framework. The question is what “influence” means and what decisions Mexico must make to keep external pressure from becoming permanent policy.

The article itself describes a relationship under pressure: more than 80% of Mexican exports go to the United States; bilateral trade is close to $900 billion, and remittances exceed $60 billion a year. It also acknowledges that Claudia Sheinbaum’s government has cooperated exceptionally, received a list of 54 trade barriers from Washington, and imposed tariffs of between 5% and 50% on products from countries without a trade agreement. According to Rubio, that decision appeared to address U.S. concerns about China.

Rubio even describes a third, quieter and more political track: Mexico would offer to buy more U.S. products, sell somewhat less, and invest more across the border. This confirms that trade relations are also used to influence Mexican decisions. Cooperation may be necessary; political consistency requires discussing its limits and defending the national interest in every negotiation.

The author says that nearly 87% of Mexican exports enter the United States duty-free and that the average effective tariff is 3.4%. That is a favorable trade position compared with other countries, but it does not eliminate the vulnerability created by sending more than 80% of our exports to a single market. That same integration also gives Mexico bargaining power: U.S. supply chains depend on the relationship with our country. Our strategy should use that interdependence to diversify, strengthen domestic production, and negotiate under clear rules.

Financial pressure can also affect Mexico directly. In June 2025, Donald Trump called for U.S. interest rates to be lowered by two to three percentage points. In September 2026, the Federal Reserve raised rates by a quarter point, to a range of 3.75% to 4%, while Banxico held Mexico’s rate at 6.50%. The differential narrowed to between 2.50 and 2.75 points, and the dollar again topped 18 pesos. That sequence may have changed the appeal of investing in pesos, put pressure on the exchange rate, and raised the cost of dollar-denominated financing. The economic effect on Mexico deserves to be assessed by its consequences, without attributing the Fed’s decision to Trump.

AMERICA'S MIDTERM ELECTIONS: TRUMP IS LOSING CONTROL OF CONGRESS

With less than three weeks until the US midterm elections on 3 November, the political winds are blowing strongly against President Donald Trump and the Republicans.

And the consequences will extend far beyond Washington...

📊 WHAT ARE THE FORECASTS SAYING?

Prediction markets currently estimate:

🔵 91% probability of Democrats winning the House of Representatives.

🔵 64% probability of Democrats winning the Senate.

🔵 63% probability of Democrats controlling BOTH chambers.

The respected Cook Political Report has also shifted numerous House races towards the Democrats, while polling-based and academic forecasts broadly agree that Republicans face a difficult election.

These aren't certainties. But the direction is unmistakable.

WHAT WOULD A DEMOCRATIC SWEEP MEAN?

If Democrats win both chambers, Trump could face two years of legislative paralysis.

❌ Major tax, spending and legislative reforms would become much harder to enact.

🔎 Congressional investigations, subpoenas and oversight of the Trump administration could intensify dramatically.

⚖️ Judicial appointments and senior administration confirmations could face significant obstacles.

💰 Budget negotiations could become increasingly confrontational, raising the prospect of further government shutdowns.

Donald Trump would retain considerable executive authority, particularly over foreign policy, regulation and immigration. But his freedom to legislate would be severely constrained.

📉 WHY ARE REPUBLICANS STRUGGLING?

Cost-of-living pressures, economic uncertainty, tariffs, the conflict with Iran and dissatisfaction with Trump's leadership are weighing heavily on Republican prospects. Trump himself suffers disapproval from 23% more respondents, over his approval rating (60% vs 37%).

History also matters: the president's party frequently suffers losses in midterm elections.

🌎 WHAT ABOUT THE REST OF THE WORLD?

A Democratic Congress could challenge Trump's trade policies, scrutinise his approach to Russia, Ukraine and the Middle East (including Iran), demand greater accountability over military operations and complicate his international agenda.

For Europe and America's other allies, this could mean greater congressional checks on Washington's decisions; but also more political uncertainty.

Government bond yields in the United States have recently been at 24-year highs. Markets could react sharply and negatively, particularly if investors anticipate legislative gridlock, increased regulation or changes in fiscal policy.

🗳️ AND THE 2028 PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION?

A Democratic victory would give the opposition momentum, visibility and institutional power heading towards 2028.

It could weaken Trump's political authority, intensify Republican debates about succession and complicate the ambitions of Vice President JD Vance and other potential Republican presidential candidates.

But Democrats would face their own test: can they offer a convincing alternative, rather than simply opposing Trump?

A Republican defeat in November would not automatically produce a Democratic president in 2028, but a switch is becoming much more likely. Betting markets show that the next Presidential race is wide open with JD Vance, AOC, Jon Ossoff, Gavin Newsom, and Marco Rubio in contention (and the Democrats are strongly favoured to win the next Presidency).

OVERALL ASSESSMENT

The most likely outcome is Democratic control of the House. The Senate remains more competitive, although betting markets now favour a Democratic victory there too...

A Democratic sweep would represent a major setback for Trump, likely transforming the final two years of his presidency into an extended struggle between the White House and Congress.

But gridlock isn't necessarily good governance. America needs effective institutions, responsible leadership, economic opportunity and a political system capable of delivering results.

The stakes are enormous for Americans, for the Western alliance, and for the wider world...

And who exactly is this “enemy” you’re talking about? Mauritius? On what evidence?

Farage told Parliament in February 2025 that Britain should sell the islands to America if sovereignty was going to be surrendered. Now he’s talking about permanent access in exchange for Trump keeping quiet about the Falklands.

Why should a prospective British Prime Minister have to bargain with an American president over another piece of British territory? Since when was respecting British sovereignty something we had to purchase from Washington?

You’ve offered no legal argument, no financial evidence and no explanation of how your proposal works. Just blind faith that Farage must be right.

So please, Daniela, explain this bigger picture you keep mentioning. Because at present it looks remarkably like you’ve confused patriotism with doing whatever Donald Trump wants.
